message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Typical Value / Description |
|----------|----------|-----------------------------|
| **Basic Identity** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | State at STP | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.9 °C (20.4 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.2 °C (14.0 K) |
| | Density (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (gas, 0 °C, 1 atm) | 22.71 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat capacity (gas, 25 °C) | 28.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.025 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Heat of fusion | 0.0005 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | 0.754 eV |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Van der Waals radius | 1.20 Å |
| | Covalent radius | 0.37 Å |
| | Polarizability | 0.666 × 10⁻²⁴ cm³ |
| | Dipole moment | 0 (non‑polar) |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.7928 µB (proton) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (¹H), 0 (²H), ½ (³H) |
| | Half‑life (³H) | 12.32 years |
| **Chemical Behavior** | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, H₂O₂, etc. |
| | Acidic strength | Strong acid when bonded to electronegative atoms (e.g., HCl, H₂SO₄). |
| | Basicity | Weak base as hydride (H⁻) or in metal hydrides. |
| | Redox behavior | Reducing agent (e.g., H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻). |
| | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds; can form diatomic H₂, hydrides, acids, and organics. |
| | Spectroscopy | Strong absorption in UV (Lyman series), visible (Balmer series), IR (stretching). |
| **Physical Behavior** | Combustion | 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (exothermic, high flame temperature). |
| | Flame color | Blue (non‑luminous). |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (low). |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Variable; often moderate in alcohols, ethers. |
| | Diffusion coefficient (air) | ~0.2 cm² s⁻¹ (fastest gas). |
| | Permeability | High through many polymers; used in gas separation membranes. |
| | Electrical conductivity | Very low in pure form; increases with ionization. |
| | Magnetic susceptibility | Diamagnetic (weakly repelled by magnetic fields). |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant (~99.98 %). |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, ~0.02 % natural abundance; heavier, lower zero‑point energy. |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay), half‑life 12.32 yr; used in nuclear fusion research. |
| **Applications** | Fuel cell fuel | H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (electrochemical). |
| | Rocket propellant | Liquid H₂ + liquid O₂ (high specific impulse). |
| | Metallurgy | Hydrogen embrittlement; used in annealing. |
| | Chemical synthesis | Hydride donors, hydrogenation catalysts. |
| | Medical imaging | ¹H NMR (MRI). |
| | Energy storage | Metal hydrides, ammonia borane, Li–H batteries. |
| | Fundamental physics | Tests of quantum electrodynamics, proton structure, gravitational redshift. |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Lightest element**: atomic mass ≈ 1 u, extremely low density.
- **Highly reactive**: forms a wide range of compounds; acts as both acid (when bonded to electronegative atoms) and base (as hydride).
- **Energy‑dense fuel**: high specific energy per mass; used in fuel cells and rockets.
- **Isotopic diversity**: stable protium, stable deuterium, radioactive tritium—each with distinct nuclear and chemical properties.
- **Spectroscopic importance**: hydrogen lines (Lyman, Balmer) are key in astronomy and plasma diagnostics.
- **Industrial relevance**: hydrogenation, metallurgy, semiconductor processing, and emerging green‑energy technologies.

Feel free to ask for deeper details on any specific property or application!
